questions.question: What are the differences between HashMap, TreeMap, and LinkedHashMap?
questions.title: Map Implementations Comparison
questions.direct_answer: **`HashMap`** gives **O(1)** average lookup with **no ordering**. **`LinkedHashMap`** keeps **insertion (or access) order** at O(1) by adding a linked list. **`TreeMap`** keeps keys **sorted** (natural or `Comparator`) using a red-black tree, at **O(log n)**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Map implementation trade-offs and when to choose each based on ordering and performance requirements
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing LinkedHashMap's insertion-order preservation with TreeMap's sorted order, or thinking all Maps have the same performance characteristics
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention LinkedHashMap's access-order mode for LRU caches and TreeMap's NavigableMap interface for range queries

sections.title: Three Map Flavors for Different Needs
sections.content: All three are **Map** implementations storing key-value pairs, but they differ in ordering guarantees and performance. **HashMap** uses hash-based storage for fast lookups with no predictable iteration order—entries appear random. **LinkedHashMap** extends HashMap and adds a doubly-linked list to maintain insertion order (or access order), so you iterate in the sequence you added entries. **TreeMap** uses a red-black tree to keep keys sorted by their natural order or a custom **Comparator**, making it perfect for range queries. Think of HashMap as a messy toolbox where you find tools instantly, LinkedHashMap as a toolbox where tools stay in the order you put them, and TreeMap as a sorted shelf where tools are alphabetically arranged.

sections.title: Map Implementations at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|HashMap|~Hash table, no order|O(1) get/put|one null key allowed|the fast default
blue|LinkedHashMap|~HashMap + linked list|O(1) get/put|insertion or access order|access-order = LRU cache
violet|TreeMap|~Red-black tree|O(log n) get/put|sorted by key, no null key|NavigableMap range queries
amber|Pick by need|~Order vs speed|no order -> HashMap|remember order -> LinkedHashMap|sorted/ranges -> TreeMap

sections.title: HashMap when iteration order actually matters
Match the Map to the ordering requirement
When to Choose Each Map
sections.content:
Use **HashMap** when you need fast key-value lookups and don't care about iteration order—think caching user sessions by sessionId or storing product prices by SKU.

Use **LinkedHashMap** when you need predictable iteration order, like displaying form fields in the order they were added, or when implementing an **LRU cache** with access-order mode.

Use **TreeMap** when you need sorted keys for range queries—finding all orders between two timestamps, or getting products in a price range. TreeMap is also useful when you want sorted iteration without explicitly sorting a list every time.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing insertion order with sorted order**: Freshers think LinkedHashMap sorts entries, but it only preserves the order you put them in—TreeMap is the one that sorts.
- **Using TreeMap for simple lookups**: Choosing TreeMap when you don't need sorting wastes memory and performance—O(log n) is slower than HashMap's O(1) for basic get/put.
- **Forgetting null key restrictions**: Trying to use null as a key in TreeMap throws NullPointerException during comparison, while HashMap and LinkedHashMap allow one null key.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **HashMap**: fastest option with O(1) operations but no iteration order guarantees
**LinkedHashMap**: extends HashMap adding insertion-order or access-order preservation via doubly-linked list
**TreeMap**: implements NavigableMap using red-black tree for O(log n) operations with sorted keys
**Access-order mode**: LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true moves entries to end on get(), perfect for LRU caches
**Null key handling**: HashMap and LinkedHashMap allow one null key, TreeMap throws NPE on null keys
**Memory trade-off**: HashMap is lightest, LinkedHashMap adds linked-list pointers, TreeMap has tree node overhead
**NavigableMap methods**: TreeMap provides floorKey(), ceilingKey(), subMap() for range operations unavailable in HashMap

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These three Maps solve different problems based on ordering needs. HashMap is your go-to for fast lookups when you don't care about iteration order—it gives you O of 1 average performance using a hash table. LinkedHashMap extends HashMap but adds a doubly-linked list to maintain insertion order, so when you iterate, entries come out in the sequence you put them in. It still has O of 1 performance but uses a bit more memory for the linked list pointers. TreeMap is fundamentally different—it uses a red-black tree to keep keys sorted, either by their natural order or a custom Comparator. This means O of log n operations, but you get powerful range query methods through the NavigableMap interface. In a real scenario, I'd use HashMap for caching user data by ID where order doesn't matter. I'd pick LinkedHashMap when building an LRU cache by setting access-order mode to true, which moves accessed entries to the end automatically. For TreeMap, imagine storing orders by timestamp—you can quickly find all orders between two dates using subMap without sorting a list. A common mistake freshers make is using TreeMap when they don't need sorting, wasting performance. Remember, LinkedHashMap preserves insertion order, it doesn't sort—that's TreeMap's job.

questions.question: How can you implement a simple LRU cache using LinkedHashMap?
questions.title: LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap
questions.direct_answer: Construct a **`LinkedHashMap`** with **`accessOrder=true`**, then override **`removeEldestEntry()`** to return `true` once `size()` exceeds your capacity. The map then auto-evicts the **least recently accessed** entry — a full LRU cache in about ten lines.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of LinkedHashMap's access-order feature and practical application of inheritance to customize collection behavior
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing LinkedHashMap has a three-parameter constructor with accessOrder boolean, or trying to implement LRU from scratch without using this feature
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the actual concise implementation—it's only a few lines and demonstrates you know this classic Java interview pattern

sections.title: LinkedHashMap's Built-in LRU Support
sections.content:
A **Least Recently Used (LRU) cache** evicts the oldest accessed entry when the cache reaches capacity, keeping frequently accessed items in memory. **LinkedHashMap** has built-in support for this pattern through its three-parameter constructor with an **accessOrder** boolean. When accessOrder is true, the map reorders entries on every get() or put() operation, moving the accessed entry to the end of the iteration sequence.

The **removeEldestEntry()** method is a protected hook you override to define when eviction happens—return true when size exceeds capacity, and LinkedHashMap automatically removes the eldest (least recently used) entry. This design eliminates manual LRU tracking logic you'd need with a plain HashMap plus a separate queue. It's elegant because the data structure itself maintains access order and handles eviction through simple subclassing.

sections.title: LinkedHashMap LRU Recipe at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Step 1|~Enable access order|super(cap, 0.75f, true)|third arg = accessOrder|default false = FIFO
emerald|Step 2|~Override the hook|removeEldestEntry(e)|return size() > capacity|called after every put
violet|How it reorders|~get/put move to tail|most recent at the end|eldest at the head|head is evicted first
amber|Caveat|~Not thread-safe|wrap synchronizedMap|or use Caffeine/Guava|production needs concurrency

sections.title: Simple LRU Cache with LinkedHashMap
When to Use LinkedHashMap for LRU
sections.content:
Use this approach when you need a simple **in-memory cache** with bounded size—caching database query results keyed by query string, or storing recently accessed user profiles by userId. It's perfect for **single-threaded** applications or when you control synchronization externally.

Use it in Spring services for lightweight caching of API responses where you want automatic eviction of old data without manual cleanup logic. It's also great for **interview scenarios** where you need to demonstrate understanding of Java collections beyond basic usage. However, for production multi-threaded caches, consider **ConcurrentHashMap** with manual LRU tracking or dedicated libraries like Caffeine or Guava Cache that handle concurrency and more sophisticated eviction policies.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting accessOrder parameter**: Using the default two-parameter constructor new LinkedHashMap(capacity, loadFactor) gives you insertion order, not access order—get() calls won't reorder entries and your LRU won't work.
- **Not overriding removeEldestEntry**: Freshers sometimes expect LinkedHashMap to auto-evict without overriding this method, but the default implementation always returns false, so nothing gets removed.
- **Ignoring thread safety**: This implementation isn't thread-safe—multiple threads calling put() or get() concurrently can corrupt the internal linked list structure, leading to ConcurrentModificationException or infinite loops.
- **Misunderstanding what eldest means**: The eldest entry is the one at the head of the iteration order (least recently accessed), not the one with the oldest value or insertion time in a general sense.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **accessOrder=true**: third parameter in LinkedHashMap constructor enables access-order mode where get() and put() move entries to tail
**removeEldestEntry()**: protected hook method called after every put()—return true to trigger automatic removal of head entry
**Eldest entry**: the entry at the head of the iteration order (least recently accessed) when accessOrder is true
**Automatic eviction**: no manual tracking needed—LinkedHashMap handles reordering and removal when removeEldestEntry() returns true
**Single-threaded**: this basic implementation isn't thread-safe—wrap with Collections.synchronizedMap() or use ConcurrentHashMap for concurrency
**Load factor**: the 0.75f parameter is the default load factor controlling when the hash table resizes internally
**Production alternative**: for real applications, use Caffeine or Guava Cache which provide thread-safe LRU with better eviction policies

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: LinkedHashMap has a special constructor that takes three parameters—capacity, load factor, and a boolean called accessOrder. When you set accessOrder to true, the map tracks access order instead of insertion order. Every time you call get or put on a key, that entry moves to the end of the iteration sequence, making it the most recently used. The eldest entry is always at the head. To make it an LRU cache, you extend LinkedHashMap and override the removeEldestEntry method. This method gets called after every put operation with the eldest entry as a parameter. You just return true when the size exceeds your capacity limit, and LinkedHashMap automatically removes that eldest entry. It's literally about five or six lines of code. For example, if you create an LRU cache with capacity three and add user colon one, user colon two, user colon three, then access user colon one, it moves to the end. When you add user colon four, the cache evicts user colon two because it's now the least recently used. One pitfall freshers hit is forgetting the accessOrder parameter and wondering why their LRU doesn't work—the default is false, which gives you insertion order. Also, this isn't thread-safe, so in production you'd need synchronization or a better library like Caffeine.

LinkedHashMap supports this natively through an access-order constructor flag — when set to true, every get or put moves the accessed entry to the end of the linked order. LinkedHashMap was designed with exactly this pattern in mind. The removeEldestEntry hook was added as an extension point specifically for LRU caches — Java's designers anticipated the use case and made it a protected method you can override.

questions.question: What are the NavigableMap methods in TreeMap and when are they useful?
questions.title: TreeMap NavigableMap Methods
questions.direct_answer: `TreeMap`'s **`NavigableMap`** methods include **`floorKey()`**/**`ceilingKey()`** (nearest key ≤/≥), **`higherKey()`**/**`lowerKey()`** (strictly adjacent), and **`headMap()`**/**`tailMap()`**/**`subMap()`** range views. They make **range queries** and **nearest-neighbor** lookups O(log n) on sorted data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of TreeMap's sorted capabilities beyond basic put/get operations and knowledge of NavigableMap interface methods
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using TreeMap only for sorted iteration without realizing it provides powerful range query operations that would be expensive with other Maps
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Provide a concrete real-world example like finding events in a time range or stock prices closest to a target value

sections.title: NavigableMap: Beyond Simple Sorted Iteration
sections.content:
**NavigableMap** is an interface that **TreeMap** implements, extending **SortedMap** with navigation methods for finding nearest keys and extracting sorted subsets.

The core power lies in **nearest-key lookups**—methods like **floorKey(K key)** return the greatest key less than or equal to the given key, while **ceilingKey(K key)** returns the least key greater than or equal. **higherKey()** and **lowerKey()** give you strictly greater or strictly less keys. The **range view methods**—headMap(), tailMap(), subMap()—return live views of portions of the map, backed by the original TreeMap so changes reflect in both. These operations are O(log n) thanks to the red-black tree structure. Without these methods, you'd have to iterate through entries or maintain separate sorted lists, which is O(n) and error-prone. NavigableMap makes TreeMap ideal for time-series data, scheduling systems, and any scenario where you query by ranges or need nearest-neighbor lookups.

sections.title: NavigableMap Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Nearest (inclusive)|~floor and ceiling|floorKey(k): largest <= k|ceilingKey(k): smallest >= k|null if none qualifies
emerald|Nearest (strict)|~higher and lower|lowerKey(k): largest < k|higherKey(k): smallest > k|excludes equality
violet|Range views|~live, backed views|headMap(k): keys < k|tailMap(k): keys >= k|subMap(from, to): [from, to)
amber|Reverse|~descending order|descendingMap()|descendingKeySet()|no manual sort needed

sections.title: Using NavigableMap for Event Scheduling
When NavigableMap Shines
sections.content:
Use **floorKey()/ceilingKey()** when you need the closest match to a target—finding the stock price at or before a specific timestamp, or getting the closest available appointment time to a requested slot.

Use **subMap()** for range queries like fetching all orders between two dates, all products in a price range, or log entries within a time window.

Use **headMap()/tailMap()** when you need everything before or after a threshold—all events before a deadline, all scores above a cutoff. These methods are efficient (O(log n)) compared to filtering a list (O(n)). In a real Spring application, you might use TreeMap to cache time-series metrics indexed by LocalDateTime, then query recent data with tailMap(). Or in a game leaderboard, store scores as keys and use descendingMap() to iterate from highest to lowest.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Iterating to find nearest**: Freshers use a loop to find the closest key instead of calling floorKey() or ceilingKey(), which is O(n) instead of O(log n) and defeats the purpose of using TreeMap.
- **Confusing floor/ceiling with higher/lower**: floorKey is less-than-or-equal-to while lowerKey is strictly-less-than—mixing these up gives off-by-one errors in range boundaries.
- **Modifying range views incorrectly**: subMap() returns a live view backed by the original TreeMap—putting an out-of-range key into the subMap throws IllegalArgumentException, which surprises freshers expecting an independent copy.
- **Not considering descending views**: Freshers forget descendingMap() and descendingKeySet() methods that give you reverse-order iteration without manual sorting.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **NavigableMap interface**: extends SortedMap with navigation methods for nearest-key and range operations
**floorKey(K)**: returns greatest key less than or equal to K, or null if none exists
**ceilingKey(K)**: returns least key greater than or equal to K, or null if none exists
**higherKey(K) / lowerKey(K)**: strictly greater/less than K without equality, useful for adjacent entries
**subMap(K from, K to)**: returns live view of keys in [from, to) range—changes reflect in both maps
**headMap(K) / tailMap(K)**: returns keys strictly less than K or greater-than-or-equal-to K respectively
**descendingMap()**: returns reverse-order view of the TreeMap, also a live view backed by original

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: TreeMap implements the NavigableMap interface, which gives you powerful methods for navigating sorted keys. The most useful ones are floorKey and ceilingKey for finding the nearest match. FloorKey returns the greatest key less than or equal to your target—think of it as the floor of your value. CeilingKey returns the least key greater than or equal to your target—the ceiling. These are O of log n operations thanks to the tree structure. Then you have higherKey and lowerKey which are strictly greater or strictly less, no equality allowed. For range queries, you use subMap to get a view of keys between two boundaries, or headMap for everything before a key, or tailMap for everything after. These return live views backed by the original TreeMap, so if you modify one, the other sees the change. A concrete example would be an event scheduling system where events are keyed by LocalDateTime. If a user asks what's the next event after three PM, you call ceilingKey with three PM and get the nearest event time at or after that. Or to get all morning events, you call headMap with noon as the boundary. A common mistake is iterating through the entire map to find the nearest key instead of using floorKey or ceilingKey, which wastes the whole point of TreeMap's sorted structure. Also, freshers forget that subMap views throw IllegalArgumentException if you try to put a key outside the range—it's not an independent copy, it's a filtered view of the original.

questions.question: What are the modern Map methods — getOrDefault(), computeIfAbsent(), and merge()?
questions.title: Modern Map Methods
questions.direct_answer: **`getOrDefault(key, default)`** returns a fallback when the key is missing. **`computeIfAbsent(key, fn)`** lazily computes and stores a value only if the key is absent. **`merge(key, value, fn)`** inserts the value or combines it with the existing one — ideal for frequency counting with `Integer::sum`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of Java 8+ Map API enhancements that make common patterns more concise and expressive
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using verbose patterns like checking containsKey() then putting, or getting then null-checking then putting, when these methods do it in one atomic operation
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show the frequency counting pattern with merge() using Integer::sum—it's much cleaner than the old get-increment-put approach

sections.title: Modern Map Methods That Replace Boilerplate
sections.content:
Java 8 added several **default methods** to the **Map interface** that eliminate common null-checking and get-then-put patterns. **getOrDefault(K key, V defaultValue)** is the simplest—it returns the value for a key, or the default if the key is missing, avoiding null checks. **computeIfAbsent(K key, Function mappingFunction)** lazily computes a value only when the key doesn't exist, then stores and returns it—perfect for initializing nested collections like Map of Lists. **merge(K key, V value, BiFunction remappingFunction)** handles both insert and update in one call—if the key is absent, it inserts the value; if present, it combines the old and new values using your function. These methods are **atomic** in the sense that they avoid the race condition of separate get-check-put operations (though they're not thread-safe without external synchronization).

They make code more declarative—you express what you want (compute if absent, merge values) rather than how to do it (check null, branch, put).

sections.title: Modern Map Methods at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|getOrDefault|~Safe read|return value or fallback|no null check needed|fallback is eager, keep it cheap
blue|computeIfAbsent|~Lazy get-or-create|runs fn only if absent|stores + returns value|grouping: Map<K,List<V>>
violet|merge|~Insert or combine|absent -> store value|present -> fn(old, new)|counting: merge(k, 1, Integer::sum)
amber|compute|~General update|v is null if absent|handle insert + update|return null removes the key

sections.title: Practical Uses of Modern Map Methods
When to Use Each Method
sections.content:
Use **getOrDefault()** when reading configuration or cache data that might be missing—you want a sensible fallback without throwing exceptions or null checks.

Use **computeIfAbsent()** when building nested data structures like grouping (Map of List) or caching expensive computations—you only pay the cost of creating the value if the key is missing. It's perfect for patterns like userMap.computeIfAbsent(userId, id -> fetchUserFromDB(id)).

Use **merge()** for aggregations like frequency counting, summing values by category, or combining maps where you need to handle both new keys and updates to existing keys in one operation. The remapping function takes oldValue and newValue, so Integer::sum for counting, String::concat for appending, or custom logic for complex merges.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using get() then null-check then put()**: Freshers write code like if (map.get(key) == null) map.put(key, new ArrayList<>()); instead of computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()), which is verbose and less readable.
- **Computing expensive values eagerly in getOrDefault()**: Calling getOrDefault(key, expensiveComputation()) always executes the default computation even if the key exists—use computeIfAbsent() for lazy evaluation.
- **Forgetting merge() for frequency counting**: Writing orderCounts.put(id, orderCounts.getOrDefault(id, 0) + 1) when merge(id, 1, Integer::sum) is cleaner and expresses intent better.
- **Confusing computeIfAbsent() with putIfAbsent()**: putIfAbsent(key, value) inserts a pre-computed value, while computeIfAbsent(key, function) computes the value lazily only if needed.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **getOrDefault(key, defaultValue)**: returns value if present, otherwise returns defaultValue—no null check needed
**computeIfAbsent(key, mappingFunction)**: computes and stores value only if key is absent, returns computed or existing value
**merge(key, value, remappingFunction)**: inserts value if key absent, otherwise combines old and new values with function
**Lazy evaluation**: computeIfAbsent() only calls the mapping function when key is missing, avoiding unnecessary work
**Frequency counting pattern**: merge(key, 1, Integer::sum) is the modern idiomatic way to count occurrences in a map
**Nested collections**: computeIfAbsent() shines for Map of List or Map of Set patterns, initializing inner collection on first access
**Thread safety**: these methods aren't atomic across multiple threads—use ConcurrentHashMap.compute methods for thread-safe operations

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These are three really useful methods that Java 8 added to the Map interface to eliminate common boilerplate. GetOrDefault is the simplest—you pass a key and a fallback value, and if the key doesn't exist, you get the fallback instead of null. It's great for configuration maps where missing keys should have sensible defaults. ComputeIfAbsent takes a key and a mapping function. If the key is absent, it calls the function to compute the value, stores it, and returns it. If the key's already there, it just returns the existing value without calling the function. This is perfect for lazy initialization of nested collections—like when you have a Map of Lists and you want to add an item but the list might not exist yet. You call computeIfAbsent to create the list only when needed. Merge is the most powerful one for aggregations. It takes a key, a value, and a remapping function. If the key is missing, it just inserts the value. If the key exists, it combines the old value and the new value using your function. The classic example is frequency counting. You can write merge with the order ID, the number one, and Integer colon colon sum. That'll increment the count if it exists or initialize it to one if it doesn't—all in one line. Before Java 8, you'd write something like get the current count, check if it's null, if so put one, otherwise put count plus one. That's way more verbose. A common mistake is calling getOrDefault with an expensive computation as the default—it always executes even if the key exists. Use computeIfAbsent for expensive operations because it's lazy.

speakable_v2.hook: Three Java 8 Map methods that each replace a common multi-line pattern — knowing them signals modern Java fluency.

beats.text: Java 8 added getOrDefault, computeIfAbsent, and merge to Map — each replacing a common verbose pattern with a single atomic method call. They're cleaner, safer, and in many cases more efficient than the pre-Java-8 equivalent because they avoid duplicate key lookups.

The old patterns — containsKey then get, get then null check then put — always made two or three separate map lookups. The new methods do the check-and-act atomically in one call, which is both cleaner and eliminates the redundant lookup.

items: getOrDefault(key, fallback): returns fallback if key is absent. Replaces the ternary map.containsKey(k) ? map.get(k) : fallback.
computeIfAbsent(key, k -> value): computes and stores the value only if key is absent, then returns it. Classic grouping pattern: map.computeIfAbsent(category, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(product).
merge(key, value, merger): if key absent, stores value. If present, applies merger(existingValue, value). Frequency counting: map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) — one line instead of three.
compute(key, (k, v) -> newValue): the general version; v is null when key is absent — handle both insert and update in one lambda.

beats.text: non-obvious: map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) is not just cleaner than map.put(word, map.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1) — it's also one map lookup instead of two. In a product catalog app counting page views per product, the merge version is both more readable and faster at scale.

items: computeIfAbsent returns the existing or newly computed value — use it as a one-step get-or-create, not just a conditional put.
merge with a null-returning merger removes the key entirely — be careful if your combiner function can return null.

speakable_v2.cap: Master merge for frequency counting, computeIfAbsent for grouping, and getOrDefault for safe reads — three patterns that cover most Java 8 Map interview questions.
